title: Fatigue Management
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Night shifts and long work hours make it hard to get enough sleep, and tired workers have a harder time focusing and are at higher risk of injury. Recognize the signs of fatigue and take action.
talking_points: Lack of sleep and long work hours can make you tired. Tired workers have a harder time focusing, which puts them at higher risk of injury.
Signs of fatigue include poor sleep, feeling tired or falling asleep at work, lack of energy or motivation, difficulty focusing, slowed reactions, and increased anger or irritability.
Take breaks at least every 1 to 2 hours, or spend time on another task.
Eat healthy snacks such as fruit and nuts. Candy, chips, and other processed and sugary foods make you feel more tired. Drink plenty of water.
If possible, stay in or go often to brightly lit areas to improve alertness.
Do not drive or operate machinery if you are overly tired. Drowsiness raises your risk of a car crash or other incident.
Rest on your days off and have at least one day off per week. Limit caffeine, especially 5 hours or more before bed.

Most people need 7 to 9 hours of quality sleep each day. Keep your sleeping space comfortable, dark, and quiet, and avoid lighted screens 60 to 90 minutes before bed. See a doctor if you have trouble sleeping or fall asleep at work.
site_hazards_to_check: Crews on long shifts or many days in a row of night work
Workers who look drowsy or are slow to react around saws, equipment, or vehicles
Operators of machinery or drivers who report being overly tired
Dim work areas during night shifts
No scheduled breaks or place to rest
discussion_questions: What are the signs that you are too tired to work safely?
What do you do to stay alert, and what makes you more tired?
Who do you tell if you are too sleepy to drive or run equipment?
